narrative: The model estimated a 59% likelihood that you will leave your job, so the promotion decision treats you as a high retention risk and denies the promotion at this time. The strongest influence in your profile actually points toward staying: your total work experience of 1–5 years is common among employees predicted to stay—about half share it—so it lowers the leave risk. That positive signal is outweighed by the second and third most influential factors. The second is that you reported having other job opportunities while in this role; only about 23% of employees predicted to stay said the same, so this strongly pushes the prediction toward leaving. The third is your relatively short time with your current organization, which also leans toward leaving. In practical terms, the model sees someone with external options and limited tenure as more likely to move on, even though your experience level alone would suggest stability. Before revisiting promotion, the organization should have a retention conversation with you about growth, transparent promotion criteria, pay and rewards, recognition, support, and workload stress. You should clarify what would make you stay and what opportunities you are considering. Addressing those retention drivers may reduce the leave risk and make a future promotion decision more supportable.
